questions.question: Explain how the Same-Origin Policy decides whether two pages are same-origin, and apply it to an HTTPS page at bank.example.com on port $443$ trying to read data from HTTPS api.bank.example.com on port $443$.
options: Reduces risk from a stolen cookie but does not stop the browser from sending that cookie on matching requests.
Encrypts the cookie value in the browser so JavaScript cannot decode it.
Prevents the server from accepting any request that lacks a CSRF token.
Restricts the cookie to only the exact URL path that created it.
questions.expected: Reduces risk from a stolen cookie but does not stop the browser from sending that cookie on matching requests.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why CSRF is possible in cookie-based web authentication?
options: Browsers automatically attach in-scope cookies to requests, so an attacker can trigger a state-changing request from another site.
Same-Origin Policy allows attacker scripts to read any response if the request uses HTTPS.
SQL injection lets the attacker overwrite all CSRF tokens in the database.
CSP disables browser cookie handling unless unsafe-inline is enabled.
questions.expected: Browsers automatically attach in-scope cookies to requests, so an attacker can trigger a state-changing request from another site.

questions.question: A NIDS processes $10{,}000$ events. There are $200$ real attacks. It raises alerts on $180$ attacks and also raises $490$ alerts on benign events. Compute true positives, false negatives, false positives, true negatives, true positive rate, false positive rate, and precision.
options: Place public-facing services such as a web server in a DMZ, restrict inbound Internet traffic to those services, restrict DMZ-to-internal traffic, and allow internal hosts controlled outbound access.
Place the database server directly on the Internet and rely on host passwords only.
Put all servers and user desktops on the same flat network behind one allow-all firewall rule.
Replace the firewall with NAT because NAT alone is equivalent to a full application-layer policy.
questions.expected: Place public-facing services such as a web server in a DMZ, restrict inbound Internet traffic to those services, restrict DMZ-to-internal traffic, and allow internal hosts controlled outbound access.

questions.question: True or false: A host-based IDS can observe process activity and local file changes that a pure network IDS may miss.
options: Validates the file extension only after upload, then stores the file under the web root.
Checks MIME type, magic bytes, size, randomized server-side name, storage outside the web root, malware scanning, and authorization before retrieval.
Trusts the Content-Type header and blocks only files larger than the browser-reported size.
Allows images to be uploaded unchanged because image formats cannot contain active content.
questions.expected: Checks MIME type, magic bytes, size, randomized server-side name, storage outside the web root, malware scanning, and authorization before retrieval.

questions.question: A site displays user comments by inserting raw comment text into the DOM with a script API that interprets HTML. Describe the attack mechanism, name the vulnerability class, and give three targeted defenses.
options: They create an encrypted point-to-point path into a network, but they can bypass perimeter visibility or expose internal services if poorly controlled.
They replace authentication because encryption proves the user is authorized.
They make malware impossible because packets are encrypted in transit.
They eliminate the need for host hardening on the destination machine.
questions.expected: They create an encrypted point-to-point path into a network, but they can bypass perimeter visibility or expose internal services if poorly controlled.

questions.question: An IDS watches a network with $1{,}000{,}000$ daily events. The attack base rate is $0.1\%$. The detector has true positive rate $99\%$ and false positive rate $1\%$. Compute expected true alerts, false alerts, and precision.

questions.question: True or false: A low false positive rate always means an IDS produces mostly useful alerts.
options: Reflected XSS depends on tricking the user into submitting a malicious request; stored XSS persists in server-side content and can affect later visitors.
Stored XSS only occurs in cookies, while reflected XSS only occurs in SQL statements.

Stored XSS requires physical network access, while reflected XSS requires ARP poisoning.

questions.question: Write pseudocode for server-side CSRF validation on a state-changing POST request. Include token generation, session storage, validation, and token rotation after success.

questions.question: Explain why broad cookie domain scope across subdomains can be dangerous. Include one example involving a weaker subdomain and one safer design choice.
options: Block all SYN packets because legitimate clients never send them.
Use SYN cookies, rate limiting, backlog tuning, upstream filtering, and scalable load balancing.
Disable TLS so the handshake uses fewer server resources.
Move the web server into the internal LAN so attackers cannot see it.
questions.expected: Use SYN cookies, rate limiting, backlog tuning, upstream filtering, and scalable load balancing.

questions.question: A DNS amplification attack sends $800$ spoofed queries per second. Each query is $60$ bytes and each response is $3{,}000$ bytes. Compute the amplification factor and the victim bandwidth in bytes per second.
options: A WLAN using weak encryption, shared passphrases, or rogue access points can enable eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks; WPA2 or WPA3, strong authentication, and certificate validation reduce risk.
Wireless networks are safe by default because radio signals cannot leave the building.
A rogue access point is harmless if it uses the same SSID as the legitimate network.
MAC filtering is sufficient because MAC addresses cannot be spoofed.
questions.expected: A WLAN using weak encryption, shared passphrases, or rogue access points can enable eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks; WPA2 or WPA3, strong authentication, and certificate validation reduce risk.

questions.question: Write pseudocode for a simple NIDS rule that detects a possible SYN flood from one source IP. Use a sliding time window, count SYN packets without matching ACK completion, and emit an alert when the count exceeds a threshold.
options: It blocks inline by default and therefore cannot merely alert.
It can prevent traffic but has no false positive risk.
